source.title: Fault-tolerant foundation models
source.authors: T. McCourt; I. Fiete; Isaac L. Chuang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out language-model loss over model size and training-token budgets, but does so under simulated hardware faults and fits a modified scaling form rather than reproducing the original studies’ setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling-law fits, coefficient trends, and loss behavior with inference-time faults. Logit temperature and scrambling results are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions’ loss-scaling behavior. The paper also cites prior scaling-law findings; those cited results are not recorded as its own results.
record.test_reason: The study trains 16 Llama2-style models (7.9e6 to 9.3e8 params, 7.9e7 to 3.5e10 tokens) and fits held-out loss surfaces in N and D. A fault-free p=0 cohort is fitted with the standard Chinchilla form. Cohorts trained under simulated hardware faults, a new training regime, need an added log-quadratic size term. These are the study's own results on the loss-scaling form, in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that fault-hardened transformers obey a modified scaling law with an extra curvature term α2. Retained capacity η/N therefore falls and then recovers with size, which they read as models learning 'good' error-correcting codes. They conjecture, without establishing it, that such models may be formally fault-tolerant at scale, and say commercial-scale runs are needed to test this. They also conclude that fault-blind models are fragile under inference-time faults, where scaling with D can reverse.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a model-size and token-budget scaling sweep with held-out text loss, but trains and evaluates models with simulated block-drop arithmetic faults; it introduces a modified scaling form and does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Fault rate changes the fitted coefficients and the observed scaling behavior. The fixed loss-floor choice affects α1: fixing E = 1.85 instead of 1.55 gives α1 ≈ 0.3 at p = 0, with no meaningful change to the other coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: Fault-blind models evaluated with inference-time faults lose monotonic improvement with training tokens. Beyond some fault rate, performance decreases with D (Fig. 3a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling with training data of clean-trained models breaks down, and can reverse, under evaluation-time computational faults.

record.problems: The largest models reach only about 10^9 parameters, and the authors state that they cannot resolve asymptotic behavior or the irreducible floor. The fitted floor is fixed because it cannot be uniquely identified from the runs. The size and token axes are not fully crossed, large models have fewer token-budget settings, and several coefficient values are available only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3b–d report logit temperature and scrambling rather than the loss-scaling measures named in the claim. Figure 2c reports the training cost of robustness, not compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

untested.parts: Compute scaling and spans beyond about 2 orders of magnitude in N. The loss floor E was not identified.
There is no check that small-run fits predict larger runs. Fig. 1 and Fig. 2c show extrapolations only, not tests.
Not tested: no compute-optimal allocation analysis.
Not tested: architecture ratios are held fixed across the ladder.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
No comparison of parameter-counting conventions, data sets, or fitting methods beyond the choice of loss floor.

missing.what: Sensitivity of α1 to the fixed loss floor: E=1.85 instead of 1.55 gives α1≈0.3 at p=0, with other coefficients unchanged.
Goodness of fit of Eq. 4 across all p cohorts, with residuals near run-to-run variation, as a basis for the V1 and V5 states.
α1, the main model-size exponent, shrinks as p increases.
Tuned hyperparameter schemes such as muP 'introduced systematic deviations from typical scaling laws'. No numbers are given.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The fault-free cohort amounts to a small near-replication of Chinchilla-form fitting, but E was fixed and the N and D axes were not fully crossed. Both main results are differential across p rather than absolute. Coefficient values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Compute scaling is not swept. The study does not establish the standard parameter-count power law for fault-hardened models; its fitted size dependence has an additional curvature term.
No test of laws fitted on small runs predicting the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation.
Architecture ratios are held fixed across the model ladder; depth and width effects are not compared.
Tests fault-hardened text pretraining only, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not compare published exponents across datasets, counting conventions, or fitting procedures generally; the fitting-choice comparison is limited to the loss floor.

rows.subject: fault-free reference cohort of Llama2-style transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out loss as a function of model size and training tokens.
rows.measure: Held-out loss scaling with model size and training tokens
rows.value: For p = 0, α2 was pinned to zero in Eq. 4; the paper uses the standard Chinchilla form for the reference cohort.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals from 1,500 bootstrap resamples per cohort; individual coefficient values are figure-only.
rows.note: The paper states that held-out loss is measured on two billion tokens and that the p = 0 cohort supplies the fault-free reference.
rows.check: The value describes the fit setup (α2 pinned to 0), not a result. The evidence that the standard form fits comes from Supp. Fig. S2, where residuals are near run-to-run variation. E was fixed at 1.55, not fitted. N spans only about two orders of magnitude.

source_check.locator_found: Methods: Dataset, Model ladder, Training, Scaling-law fits; Fig. 2 caption; Supplementary Fig. S2.

rows.subject: fault-hardened Llama2-style transformer cohorts
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out loss against model size and training tokens separately for fault-rate cohorts.

conditions.value: p > 0; rates sampled among seventeen values from 0 to 0.2

rows.value: For p > 0, Eq. 4 adds a model-size curvature coefficient α2; the paper reports that this term lets fault-hardened models close the performance gap to fault-free counterparts as size grows.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals from 1,500 bootstrap resamples per cohort.
rows.locator: Eq. 4; Fig. 2; Supplementary Materials, sections B–C
rows.note: The fitted model-size term is not a single power law in N when α2 is nonzero. The paper says the curvature-free Chinchilla fit fails for p > 0.
rows.check: Training under faults is a different regime, so this bears on V5, not V1. Drop V7: the bend comes from a regime change, not a setup or fitting choice. Under faults the size term is log-quadratic rather than a single power law, and the standard form 'fail[s] miserably' (Supp. C). The data term keeps power-law form.

rows.subject: fault-hardened Llama2-style transformer cohorts
rows.operation_detail: Report the model-size curvature coefficient α2 across independently fitted fault-rate cohorts.
rows.value: Figure only; the text states α2 grows with p, then plateaus at large p.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals from 1,500 bootstrap resamples per cohort.
rows.locator: Fig. 2a; Results, The scaling behavior of fault-hardened transformers
rows.note: The nonzero curvature at p > 0 is evidence against a single model-size power law in this tested faulted setting; exact coefficient values are not given in the text.
rows.check: The state 'absent' is wrong. α2 is nonzero for p>0, grows with p and then plateaus, which is a measured departure from a pure power law in N. Drop V1 and V7 for the same reasons as R2. Values are in Fig. 2a only.

rows.subject: fault-hardened Llama2-style transformer cohorts
rows.operation_detail: Report the training-data coefficient β1 across fault-rate cohorts.
rows.baseline: Fault-free reference coefficient value not stated.
rows.value: Figure only; the text states β1 decreases as p increases. Eq. 4 retains an exponential-in-log-tokens data term.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals from 1,500 bootstrap resamples per cohort.
rows.note: The text describes a power-law-form data term in token count, with its coefficient varying with fault rate.
rows.check: The data term e^{β0−β1 ln(D/D0)} is a power law in D in every cohort, including faulted ones. β1 falls with p. Drop V1 except for the p=0 cohort, which R1 already covers. Values are in Fig. 2b only.

rows.subject: fault-blind Llama2-style transformer, width 512 and depth 13
rows.stage_stated: pretraining without faults; evaluated with inference-time faults
rows.operation_detail: Measure held-out performance across training-token budgets and inference-time fault rates.

conditions.value: eight budgets spanning two orders of magnitude

rows.measure: Held-out loss/performance versus training-token budget under inference-time faults
rows.baseline: The expected reference is performance increasing monotonically with training tokens; exact baseline values are not stated.
rows.value: Figure only; the text states that scaling with training duration weakens as peval increases and can reverse beyond a fault-rate threshold.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error from eight independently trained models for each D value.
rows.locator: Fig. 3a; Results, Fault-blind models collapse under inference-time errors
rows.note: The paper does not state the threshold or individual loss values in text.
rows.check: These models were trained clean and evaluated with inference-time faults. That is a train/eval mismatch under corruption, not the held-out pretraining loss scaling the versions name. The measure is 'performance' in Fig. 3a, and the threshold and values are not given in text.

relationships.reason: The standard Chinchilla form fits the p=0 cohort with residuals near run-to-run variation (R1; Supp. Fig. S2). This holds only with E fixed at 1.55.
relationships.display_finding: The Chinchilla form fits with residuals near run-to-run variation when the loss floor E is fixed at 1.55.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R1: the standard form fits the fault-free cohort; Supplementary Fig. S2 reports residuals near run-to-run variation. The fit fixes E=1.55 and α2=0; this does not establish that other floor choices fail.

relationships.condition: Training-token dependence under fault-hardened training (p up to 0.2)
relationships.reason: The data term keeps power-law form in D in every fault cohort, with an exponent that falls as p rises (R4).
relationships.display_finding: The data term retains power-law form across fault cohorts through p = 0.2, while its exponent decreases as fault probability rises.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Training-token dependence under fault-hardened training (p up to 0.2)
source_check.reason: Eq. 4 retains a power-law data term, and Fig. 2b reports β1 decreasing with fault rate. Supplementary Fig. S2 supports the fitted form across measured cohorts.

relationships.condition: Model-size dependence under fault-hardened training, p>0
relationships.reason: The curvature-free form fails for p>0. The size term needs a log-quadratic α2 that grows with p, so the single power law does not carry over (R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: For positive fault probability, the curvature-free form failed and required a log-quadratic model-size term whose coefficient increased with fault probability.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Model-size dependence under fault-hardened training, p>0
source_check.reason: For this condition group, Supplementary Sec. C explicitly reports failure of the standard Chinchilla form and systematic curved residuals. Eq. 4 requires a log-quadratic size term, contradicting V5's same-power-law-form claim for model-size dependence.

relationships.condition: Choice of the fixed loss floor E in the fits
relationships.reason: From the text, not the rows: E cannot be identified from these runs. Fixing E=1.85 instead of 1.55 changes α1 to about 0.3 at p=0.
relationships.display_finding: The runs could not identify E; fixing it at 1.85 instead of 1.55 changed α₁ to about 0.3 at p=0.
